title: Translucency perception: A review
authors: Gigilashvili, D., Thomas, J.-B., Hardeberg, J. Y., & Pedersen, M. (2021)
review_question: To overview the knowledge status about the visual perception of translucency, highlight its applications, and summarize current knowledge gaps, challenges, and ambiguities to facilitate future research.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Not explicitly defined; the review focuses on recent developments and knowledge status in translucency perception research.

findings.quote: the HVS relies on the low-level image cues for calculating translucency.

findings.antecedent: object scale, color saturation, specular reflections
findings.quote: They examined and described different factors, such as object scale, color saturation, and the presence of specular reflections, potentially affecting perceived translucency.
some regions, such as edges, contain richer information regarding material translucence.

findings.consequent: differentiation between translucent and opaque materials
findings.quote: The intensities of the shadowed regions seem to be one of the most significant visual characteristics differentiating translucent and opaque materials.

findings.antecedent: blurring and decreased contrast in nonspecular regions of opaque material
findings.quote: blurring and decreasing the contrast in the nonspecular regions of the opaque material generates a translucent look.

findings.antecedent: lack of covariance between shape and shading information
findings.quote: the lack of covariance between the shape and shading information correlates well with the perceptual translucency.
translucency perception is anatomically independent from color and texture perception.

findings.antecedent: smaller object scale / thin parts of object
findings.quote: Photons need to travel a shorter distance at the edges – making them bright and thus, a characteristic cue for distinguishing translucent and opaque materials
surface roughness... blurs the background image and evokes the perception of translucency
presence of sharp edges make materials appear less translucent.

findings.antecedent: caustic patterns cast by an object onto another surface
findings.quote: caustic patterns that are cast by an object onto another surface... might be the only indicator of translucency
motion relative to the illumination has a considerable impact on the luminance distribution on the object body and makes perception of translucency more convincing.
perceived translucency of painted citrus fruits is significantly correlated with their color saturation.
glossiness might be increasing perceived magnitude of translucency.

findings.antecedent: luminance information alone or spatial information alone
findings.quote: neither luminance nor spatial information alone is enough for estimating perceived translucency. The HVS seemingly uses some sophisticated combination of the both.

findings.antecedent: shadowed regions (looking brighter in translucent materials)
findings.quote: The regions which are usually shadowed in opaque objects are also informative about translucency, as they look brighter in translucent materials.

people estimate absorption and scattering properties better in the stimuli existing in reality than in synthetic, virtual materials proposedly attributed to a better training and experience with interacting with the real materials.

synthesis_conclusions: Translucency is among the most essential visual attributes of appearance, yet remains one of the least studied.
The knowledge about the visual mechanisms of translucency perception remains limited, with no model yet able to accurately and robustly predict perceived translucency.
Accurate prediction of translucent object appearance has significant commercial impact, particularly in fields like 3D printing.
Advances in computer graphics techniques have facilitated translucency perception research by enabling easier generation of translucent visual stimuli.
The visual cues and perceptual mechanisms for transparency (see-through filters) are fundamentally different from those for translucency (highly scattering, non-see-through media).
Multiple factors contribute to perceived translucency, including illumination direction, object structural thickness, and subsurface scattering properties.

The human visual system likely infers translucency from luminance distribution around edges, in shadowed regions, and its covariance with surface geometry, as well as apparent contrast and blur when a background is visible.
Overall translucency perception research is still in its infancy, hindered by problems with conceptual understanding, comprehension of the term, and reproducibility of tasks.
Future research using eye tracking experiments and neuroscience could reveal significant image regions, cues, and underlying anatomical mechanisms for translucency perception.
evidence_gaps: The knowledge about the visual mechanisms of translucency perception remains limited.
Little is known how the optical properties of a material relate to a perception evoked in humans.
The exact visual and cognitive mechanisms of translucency perception are far from being fully understood.
No model has yet been able to predict perceived translucency of a given material in an accurate and robust manner.
How the passage of light through a material relates to a visual sensation of translucency remains unclear.
No technique has been proposed for instrumental measurement of perceptual translucency.
The question of how exactly absorption and scattering coefficients contribute to the perceptual correlate of translucency remains largely unresolved.
The perceptual dimensions of translucency are not known, and its relation with transparency and opacity remains fuzzy.
No study has investigated translucency perception on fluorescent materials.
How well the HVS can separate light emerging from a material into transmitted and emitted components, or whether humans can differentiate between translucent and fluorescent stimuli, is unknown.
The role of the refractive index in the appearance of non-see-through materials remains understudied.
The impact of illumination structure on the perception of translucency is not well-explored.
Whether the absence of caustics or the impact of the ambient surface on overall object luminance solely attributes to perceived translucency needs further research.
The role of familiar materials identification and other psychological priors in translucency perception is unclear.
How the HVS uses motion and scene dynamics to assess translucency is unknown.
The physiology of translucency perception from retinal to cortical levels and its individual variability are not well understood.
The exact mechanisms of translucency perception remain largely unidentified.
Which image cues and regions the HVS relies on, and how it identifies, calculates, and weights them, is unknown.
The role of shape and geometry perception and how the HVS calculates them is not fully understood.
The extent to which perceived translucency is impacted by other appearance attributes such as color, gloss, texture, and fluorescence is unclear.
The lack of knowledge on how to quantify translucency makes it challenging to measure it by magnitude estimation and psychophysical scaling methods.
There is a lack of standardization for normal conditions of observing translucency and a standard observer definition.
Knowledge about cross-individual differences in translucency perception is virtually nonexistent.
limitations: The exact visual and cognitive mechanisms of translucency perception are far from being fully understood.
No model has yet been able to predict perceived translucency of a given material in an accurate and robust manner.
The exact meaning of translucency is not universally accepted and remains subjective, hindering scientific communication and research advancement.
The lack of knowledge on how to quantify translucency makes it challenging to use magnitude estimation and psychophysical scaling methods.
The inconstancy of translucency across different shapes makes it challenging to separate translucency as a material property from object property.
It is difficult to estimate optical properties of a material and decouple its visual appearance from shape-related effects.
The task of assessing translucency is inherently ambiguous, with cues varying across object regions, making observers uncertain about which region to assess.
Pivotal limitations of experimental methods include constraints related to visual stimuli selection (real objects, photographs, CGI).
Physical objects are difficult and expensive to model, measure, and replicate, and experiments with them take longer, risk damage, and have limited reproducibility.
There is a lack of standardization for normal observation conditions and a standard observer definition.
Varying viewing conditions (distance, visual field size) across experiments complicate comparative analyses.
Knowledge about cross-individual differences in translucency perception is virtually nonexistent.

Eye-tracking has limitations: fixations might be unrelated to translucency, parafoveal vision and non-local cues are not captured, temporal resolution might be insufficient, and equipment presence might affect natural interaction.
